chunks: From him, from Hammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, from al-Husayn ibn Abdillah, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'We are in the mountain, so we send the shepherds to the sheep, and perhaps the sheep becomes sick or something affects it, so they slaughter it and we eat it.' He said: 'It is merely a slaughtered animal, so one cannot be certain of its purity except if it is slaughtered by a Muslim.'

key_terms.الذَّبِيحَةُ: The slaughtered animal; here used to denote an animal slaughtered but whose status may be uncertain regarding purity or validity.
key_terms.الرُّعَاةَ: The shepherds; specifically those tending the livestock.
key_terms.الْمُسْلِمُ: The Muslim; one whose faith guarantees the validity and purity of their ritual slaughter in this context.
key_terms.عَطِبَتِ: It became sick or afflicted with a minor ailment.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating meat slaughtered by non-Muslim shepherds in remote areas?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that meat slaughtered by non-Muslim shepherds in remote areas is considered merely 'dhabeeha' (slaughtered) but not guaranteed halal due to the uncertainty of their ritual validity. This ruling highlights the Shia principle of 'istishab al-hurmiyah' (presumption of prohibition) when the status of the slaughterer's faith or ritual precision is in doubt, distinguishing it from the meat of the People of the Book which is explicitly permitted in the Quran.
